name: Delcy Rodríguez
role: Acting president of Venezuela (since January 2026); previously vice president (2018–2026), foreign minister, Constituent Assembly president, economy and oil minister
summary: A long-time chavista official who led Venezuela's foreign ministry, the 2017 Constituent Assembly and, from 2018, the vice presidency, and who became acting president after the US detained Nicolás Maduro in January 2026. Her record combines sovereigntist, anti-sanctions and anti-interference rhetoric with, in 2026, an oil-sector opening to private and foreign investors, cooperation with the United States, an amnesty law and a promise of elections. Her stated positions on social and cultural questions are largely unrecorded in the sources reviewed.

public-ownership.rationale: She signed the 2026 law ending PDVSA's monopoly and opening production and sales to private firms, while the state keeps ownership of reserves and PDVSA remains. Mixed evidence.

restrict-hate-speech.rationale: She presided over the Constituent Assembly that passed the 2017 anti-hate law (10 to 20 years for promoting hatred), but in September 2026 she asked for a partial reform to decriminalize its offences, saying it had been abusively applied, while ruling out repeal. Evidence points both ways.

drastic-climate-action.rationale: At the 2026 UN General Assembly she criticized forced decarbonization projects as risking industrial collapse, employment and food security in oil-producing countries; she did not address government action on climate change as such.

state-directs-investment.rationale: In October 2026 she defended measures to direct bank credit toward productive and industrial sectors.

nature-intrinsic-value.rationale: At the 2026 UN General Assembly she called for respect for 'los derechos de la naturaleza' (rights of nature).

expand-fossil-fuels.rationale: As acting president she signed the January 2026 reform of the Hydrocarbons Law to attract private and foreign oil investment and raise output, forecast higher oil investment, and called the 2026 US-Venezuela oil agreement one of the largest ever signed.

constituent-assembly.rationale: She presided over the 2017 Constituent Assembly and defended it as having power to act; opponents boycotted its election and disputed its legitimacy, so whether it fits 'democratically elected' is contested.

non-intervention.rationale: As Constituent Assembly president (2017) she said Venezuelans would resolve their crisis 'sin ningún tipo de interferencia extranjera', and at the 2026 UN General Assembly she said some countries try to interfere in Venezuela's affairs; she spoke of aggression aimed at intervention (2017 UN HRC). The statement is absolute ('for any reason'), which she did not address.

restructure-world-economy.rationale: At the 2017 UN Human Rights Council she called for a new international order limiting the financial powers she blamed for poverty and inequality.

national-resource-control.rationale: The 2026 reform she signed keeps hydrocarbon reserves state-owned but lets private and foreign firms run fields and sell crude, including with less than a majority stake, and allows international arbitration. Earlier chavista rhetoric stressed sovereignty; her most recent record favours foreign participation. Contested.

notes: Positions changed sharply after January 2026: she now cooperates with the US, thanks Trump, and promotes private and foreign oil investment, while still calling Maduro the legitimate president (NBC interview). Dollarization: rejected in 2021 and again in October 2026. Gaza: in 2023 she called Israel's offensive genocide, but no statement matches a current statement in the test. Essequibo: she asserts Venezuelan rights under the 1966 Geneva Agreement and asks Guyana to drop the ICJ case; no test statement fits cleanly, so it is left null. Her 2024 claim that opposition tally sheets were forged is a government position on a specific dispute and is not used for any statement. Unreachable: NPR amnesty article (timeout), El Colombiano (redirect loop), a mirror of a Sputnik piece on ties with China/Russia (connection refused), the later half of Wikipedia (no body text).
